#1099. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

Michael Carrick believes it's possible to emulate Sir Alex Ferguson's success at Manchester United, but accepts he won't be given as much time to turn the club's fortunes around as his former boss.

On the 40th anniversary of Ferguson replacing Ron Atkinson in 1986 with United one place above the relegation zone, Carrick's team are in an identical position having equalled Atkinson's club record worst start of one win from the first nine games.

A rousing win over Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday has lifted the mood around Old Trafford and eased some of the pressure on Carrick ahead of Sunday's game at home to Aston Villa.

Ferguson survived a barren three-and-a-half years in charge before winning the FA Cup in 1990. It was the first over 38 trophies over more than quarter of a century, and Carrick was asked if it would be impossible to match that.

'Well, it's not impossible,' said Carrick. 'Anything's possible. You've got to build, you know. You've got to be realistic. You've got to put things in perspective as well. The recent history that we've had and where we want to get to, it's not going to happen in a blink of an eye. It's not going to happen overnight. Success does take time, and we don't like having to spend time. But it does take a period of time to build.'

Asked if he will be given the same amount of time as Ferguson after 10 months in charge, Carrick replied: 'The game's certainly changed, no doubt. It always does. It had evolved to the stage probably after Sir Matt (Busby) in the years after that, to then Sir Alex.

'It evolves all the time. That's how it is. It changes. We've got to deal with what's in front of us. I get the comparisons. I understand it. There are always different things to compare, but it's we've always got to live in the present as well.

Michael Carrick accepts he won't be given time to emulate Sir Alex Ferguson at Man United

'Definitely use past experiences to help us, but we're all desperate to win football matches and win them as quickly as you possibly can.'

It was suggested that the 3-2 comeback win over Roma could be Carrick's 'Mark Robins moment' in reference to the striker's FA Cup winner against Nottingham Forest that was said to have saved Ferguson from the sack.

'More comparisons, yeah,' smiled Carrick. 'You always find something to compare, don't you? It's up to us to take it forward, you know. It was a fantastic night.

'It was nice for the supporters to end like that and to have that feeling, one hundred per cent for sure.

'But nothing's achieved yet, and it's one moment really in time that we need to use to move forward. But we need more of it, for sure.'

On Ferguson's 40th anniversary at United and his relationship with the Scot these days, Carrick said: 'What has not been said already? It's something definitely worth celebrating as a football club. That it's 40 years this week since he came here, and the impact on the football club, moving forward for all the time that he was here and that he's left for others to carry forward is incredible.

'I'm probably closer to him now and speak more to him now than I did when I was playing. I think the relationships change over time and that's only natural. Ever since I came here, the impact he had on me as an individual was immense.

#1091. Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

#1089. AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

James Zou is in the Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305, USA.

Artificial intelligence has been tremendously useful in science, but, most of the time, it is used for computational work, such as analysing data, making predictions and scouring literature. Carrying out ‘wet laboratory’ experiments — which involve handling liquids, biological material and chemicals — is another matter. An AI system might design a promising biologically active molecule in minutes, but testing it can take weeks or months and requires extensive human effort. In a paper published in Nature, Wu et al.1 introduce AutoDNA, a lab in which AI agents plan and conduct molecular-biology experiments involving DNA, with relatively little human intervention. The work shows how AI systems can begin to close the gap between proposing an experiment and doing it.

It started just minutes after touchdown in Turkey.

In a taxi journey across Istanbul's intercontinental bridge to Fenerbahce's stadium, the driver took a break from lighting up a cigarette or shouting profanities at other road users. He turned, looked me in the eye, and asked: 'You know Mohamed Salah?'

Two and a half hours after fighting through mind-blowing traffic (think your gridlocked motorway at 5pm multiplied by 100), on arrival at Liverpool's press conference, one gentleman did not even exchange pleasantries. He shoved a selfie stick in my face and asked about Salah.

And these two encounters were 650 miles away from where the Egyptian player now plies his trade. This fandom was only a starter when compared to the main course of Salahmania that greeted us upon arrival in the port city of Trabzon, to the east of Turkey on the coast of the Black Sea.

Here, his face and name were everywhere you looked. 'You come for Salah?' enquired the hotel receptionist. Upon hearing that was indeed the purpose of the visit, he upgraded the room to a superior suite overlooking the ocean. Result.

The streets of this city, which feels a world apart from the bustling metropolis of Istanbul, never mind Liverpool, are packed with antique dealers, and markets selling two-foot-long fish for less than £1 and the local delicacy of hamsi (anchovy to you and me).

Mohamed Salah can relax in Trabzon and has taken multiple hiking trips in the highlands (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Fans have now taken to posing at the same spots Salah appeared at - such is their hero worship

Everywhere you turned, there was a nod to Salah. His name was heard in conversations as the melodic call to prayer rang out from the nearby Hagia Sophia mosque, his picture seemed to be hung from every building and his name was on the back of every shirt being sported in town.

Shops were selling mugs, scarves, plates, masks and even cigarette lighters shaped like Salah.

At the futuristic waterfront stadium known as Papara Park, Salahmania continued - with punters putting on impromptu barbecues and DJ sets from beside their cars similar to tailgates in American sports. Everyone in this city was dancing to the beat of the Egyptian King.

Fans, many in Trabzonspor-coloured jester hats with bells on, glowed about Salah. Most do not speak a word of English in this city not far from the Armenian and Georgian border. But those who could summed up the mood.

'We love him, he is going to make us champions,' said one.

Another told us: 'People across the country now support Trabzonspor and people come from other countries, people want us to win just because of Mohamed Salah.'

Trabzonspor supporters told Daily Mail Sport: 'We love him, he is going to make us champions'

Everywhere you turned there was a nod to Salah in his new club's kit

There were plenty of children in the crowd, and more women than expected. Some had come from afar to see him, others could not believe that Salah had chosen their team and hometown.

So, why Trabzon? Why did Salah choose this project in Turkey's 30th biggest city? Why not one of the three Istanbul giants – Fenerbahce, Galatasaray or Besiktas – who have won 28, 27 and 21 Turkish titles respectively, compared to Trabzonspor's seven, including only one since 1984.

The answers are obvious, according to sources. Salah, now 34, wanted a place where he could enjoy his football without the intense scrutiny. Every word and facial expression would generate days of news coverage in Liverpool or Istanbul or another one of Europe's giant cities.

On the outskirts of Trabzon, Salah can relax, hiking up to a group of boulders in Yayla. Even there, he's worshipped, though. Trabzonspor fans flock there to pose for photographs on the same rock where he sat for a photo posted on his Instagram.

Salah's family are settled, he is becoming obsessed with chess and he has started drinking the Turkish salted-yoghurt drink ayran each day.

On the pitch, there is a belief Trabzonspor can beat the big three and end Galatasaray's four-year grip on the title.

The team also stars former Liverpool midfielder Fabinho and ex-Manchester United goalkeeper Andre Onana, while Jerome Boateng, once a stalwart at Bayern Munich, is assistant manager. Boss Thomas Reis was poached from Ludogorets and has lost just once since his arrival.

Salah is settled with his family and faces less scrutiny than in Istanbul or Liverpool (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted five more in his 15 games in Turkey so far

The highlight so far came on September 19, when Salah scored a hat-trick in a 4-0 thumping of Galatasaray. Trabzonspor have won seven league games in a row and will aim to go deep in the Conference League despite Thursday's undeserved 1-0 defeat to Freiburg.

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted in five more in his 15 games in Turkey.

'Everyone wants to work with a star the size of Mohamed Salah,' striker Paul Onuachu, once of Southampton, told us after that game. 'He is a top guy and a world star.

'He adds so much to us and helps all of us, thanks to his experience and quality, and he contributes positively to the development of our team.

'I am grateful for him. It is a blessing to play with him.'

Salah did not have the rub of the green in the clash with the German side, who were Europa League finalists last year. But a trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon and not any of his other mega-money offers.

A man wearing Trabzonspor's claret and light blue colours shows off his support for Salah

A trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon

He had approaches from America, and the Saudi Arabian federation tried to sign him right until the day he jetted into Trabzon - where he was greeted by 35,000 fans with fireworks and flares. Besiktas held advanced talks with Salah's agent Ramy Abbas.

But Trabzonspor won the race and Salah is playing with a smile again, even though that face pulled a bit of a grimace when he spotted a familiar face or two from the English press pack waiting for him after the game.

His laugh faded into an expression that said: 'I thought I got rid of you lot pestering me!'

That face confirmed his reason for joining Trabzonspor: Salah is out of the spotlight – certainly while still in with a chance to win trophies and maintain a good level of football until next summer's Africa Cup of Nations.

After a public fall-out with Liverpool that saw the final year of his contract ripped up and him accuse the Anfield club of 'throwing him under the bus', it feels like Salah is feeling at home and happy again.

It's not difficult to turn down the multiple opportunities to buy Salah-branded magnets or shirts or teddies or socks or lighters as we bid farewell to Trabzon, but it is hard to escape the conclusion that the feeling of love is mutual in this football-mad city.

#1084. Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

#1083. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

Estevao continues to be lively and should have been rewarded a couple of minutes ago with an assist when standing up a cross for Neto who loops his header tamely at Lammens.

Cunha meets a good cross from Bruno Fernandes with an air-kick. Pffft.

TNT’s team are raving about the goal and while Rogers did very well, Andrey Santos and Baleba both missed tackles and Yoro was nowhere.

Chelsea 1 Man Utd 0 (Rogers) Lavía wins the ball off Mbeumo in the centre-circle and beats Baleba who slid into a tackle, knocking it past him and on to Rogers. The England forward dipped his shoulder and set off on a run down the inside-left channel. Yoro, out of position, left a gap that Maguire felt he had to fill. Rogers diddled him with bodyswerve, dinked the ball away from Martinez and chipped the keeper. Nice finish. Terrible defending.

The absolute inertia of Manchester United’s defence laid bare. A cute finish from Morgan Rogers but in attacking the back four he barely needed to deviate from a straight line.

“We’ve had really good chances, played very well. We’ve done a lot of good things. The game’s always in the balance here. We need to take our chances. We need a big second half.”

A very entertaining game between two lively if markedly flawed teams. Manchester United probably shaded that half but have had a tendency to wilt in the second half of games and will be hacked off not to be ahead. With Chelsea the absence of Joao Pedro hits hard. Creatively they have more than enough in Estevao, Neto and Rogers (Palmer has been quiet), but no one either to occupy Martínez constantly or finish things off.

Palestra and Fofana could do with a double espresso, two Red Bulls and maybe a couple of Rothmans rather than oranges and half-time tea. They keep nodding off.

End to end and after Neto misses a golden opportunity after scything the right side of Man Utd’s defence open by spraying a shot/cross through the six-yard box, Estevao is put through by Lavia’s pass. Instead of squaring it to Neto he pumps his shot straight at Lammens.

Two more than decent attacks, two very wobbly defences.

Palestra might as well by wearing pyjamas. Caught asleep again he lets Amad go down the right. Fofana’s header from a right-wing corner hits Caicedo’s hand and trickles on to the post.

Palestra, Caicedo and Colwill let Amad go down the inside right to receive the pass from Cunha. Again Amad tightens the angle and has his cross looking for Mbeumo lumped behind for a corner.

A well-worked corner routine almost pays off for Man Utd. No reward this time but Chelsea look very shaky defending set-pieces after hiring Austin McPhee.

Even in an open game, with gifts of chances for both Bruno Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo, United supporters continue to make their disenchantment clear. The latest disobliging chants about Jim Ratcliffe, Jason Wilcox and the suggested new stadium are on a continuous loop.

No goal. Cunha was offside when nodding it Maguire’s set-up from five yards. He was offside but was also bumped there by a Chelsea defender.

Fofana who cost a fortune and, even given mitigation of injuries, has been a bust so far, dozes on the ball, has his pocket picked by Amad and makes partial amends by pushing Amad so wide that his shot eventually comes from the tightest of angles and allows Penders to block it, sending it behind with his foot.

Amad dinks the ball to Bruno Fernandes on a right-wing overlap and darts infield. Bruno threads a pass back to him and he cuts on to his left and hammers a low shot arrowing towards the bottom right that Penders parries to Mbeumo about a yard in from the byline. He opens his body to try to pass to Cunha who slides in to shoot and the ball is deflected out for a corner.

The visitors are playing well on the break but have just again been let down by a lack of an assured touch or confident thinking, Mbeumo giving up too early on Baleba’s astute pass.

Jason Wilcox, according to the travelling support, has a hobby that is said to threaten his eyesight.

Manchester United flood forward on the break with Mbeumo bombing down the inside-left before sliding a fine pass through to Cunha whose first touch is frankly dreadful, ruing a great break and opportunity by prodding it beyond his reach to Penders.

Acheampong, Estevao and Caicedo combine with a slick passing move down the right to earn another corner. Colwill’s header sets up a defender’s lashed shot that is scuffed straight at Lammens.

That’s a big chance spurned by Bruno Fernandes. A swift United counter attack and for a moment it looked like Bryan Mbeumo had delayed his switch pass too long but it finds its way to Fernandes. His first touch isn’t the best and he sends his shot flying over the crossbar.

The ball ricochets around the box from what looked like more dodgy handling by Lammens but Man Utd clear and send Mbeumo off sprinting down the right. He takes the ball 50 yards then sees Bruno’s parallel run down the inside left, bends a wonderful pass into his stride and the captain meets it with his left, blazing over from 18 yards.

Rogers gallops forward down the left after winning the ball off Amad but when he feeds it inside to Palmer, Yoro had followed the Chelsea playmaker and nicked it off him. Chelsea win it back and Rogers, manipulating the ball from right foot to left and back again, earns his side a corner on the left.

Estevao punishes Lammens handling mistake when dealing with a right wing cross by tapping the ball into an open goal at the back post but he was a yard offside.

Twice in a minute Estevao eludes Dalot down the right with his trickery and control but his first cut-back is read by Maguire and cleared and his second by Andrey Santos.

Neat move by Manchester United down their left with Dalot pushing Acheampong back with an enterprising dribble. He picks up his head and works the ball to Cunha who lays it off to Bruno Fernandes. The captain sees Santos striding forward like the great Carlos Alberto and tees him up perfectly for a shot on the run but steers it wide with his left from 20 yards.

Lavia tries to surprise Lammens with a quick free-kick from 50 yards but the keeper backpedals to take a comfortable catch. Who does he think he’s playing for? Brighton?

Man Utd lose possession from Lammens kick out and Estevao tacks in off the right wing on to his left, wraps his instep around a shot but flays it wide of the left post. Not enough bend.

Bruno loses the ball in a duel with Lavia but Baleba is there in support and works the ball out to Amad running down the right. He slides a pass into the box to Cunha who flicks it between Colwill’s legs but too heavily and Penders rushes out to gather before Cunha could run round the other side to set up a shot.

TNT Sports points out that Chelsea’s average age is 24 and Neto, at 26, is the oldest player. Palestra, pushed high on the left, works a triangle with Rogers and Palmer that sends the No 10 to the byline but his cross is blocked by Maguire.

Interesting that after the minute’s silence Harry Maguire was the only United player who went over to applaud the United fans before kick-off. The players got a brutal reception last weekend against Bournemouth at Old Trafford and there’s huge pressure on them here to deliver a response as an embattled Michael Carrick desperately tries to breathe life into their season.

The away fans are in good voice and their team have started playing with some confidence, zipping the ball around and tackling tigerishly. A but too tigerish from Amad who is penalised for catching Caicedo.

Man Utd kick off and chip it long, looking for an Mbeumo flick-on but he’s surrounded. Looks like Pedro Neto is the false nine for Chelsea with Rogers on the left.

And a round of applause, both sides go into their huddles. A Chelsea Pensioner walks over to the Manchester United dug out and shakes Carrick’s hand.

The players come out but there will also be a commemoration of Remembrance in Chelsea’s last home match before 11/11. There are representatives from the armed forces forming a guard of honour and holding a banner in the centre-circle depicting a poppy and the Chelsea lion.

There’s no hiding from the fact that we need to win games. Today’s another opportunity. It’s a tough game [but] we are coming down here to try to win the three points. We’ve done it before. We have prepared well and trained well. The boys are ready.

Of course Bruno is an important player. He has proved it for quite some time. When we get the best version of him he proved last season what he can do as he has proved for so long at this football club. And he will do it again that’s for sure.

Experience helps [talking about importance of Maguire] and we’ve got a good balance in the group. The boys are going in to this game in a clear mind about what we need to do.

It’s more about us [when asked what he thinks Chelsea’s strengths are], what we bring to the game ourselves. We can’t control what they can bring to the game. We have to be the best versions of us and if we’re close to that we’ve got a good chance of winning the game.

Today is a big one. We need a good game and a good performance. We expect a tough game, and intense game against United. They are a big team and good players, so we will need our best.

[Estevao is starting] because he is ready, because he has been preparing and training well. Today he is needed, and we hope he enjoys his game and that he can have a good impact.

Jordan [Henderson] is ill, no injury, but he was not feeling well yesterday, and today he had a fever.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

We know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

If there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.
